analysis.one_liner: Bans the use of hydrofluoric acid at oil refineries within five years to prevent mass-casualty releases.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: About 40 U.S. oil refineries use hydrofluoric acid, a dangerously corrosive chemical, to make high-octane gasoline. If a refinery leak, accident, or attack released a large cloud of it, the bill's findings say it could kill or permanently injure thousands of people living within 25 miles, and more than 14 million people live near these refineries. The bill would ban new refineries from using the chemical immediately and give existing refineries five years to switch to safer, already commercially proven methods. It was referred to committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: The more than 14 million people living in communities around refineries that use hydrofluoric acid, plus refinery workers, who would no longer face the risk of a mass-casualty chemical release. The bill's findings note many of these communities already carry disproportionate environmental burdens.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any new refinery from using hydrofluoric acid starting on the day the law takes effect, and gives existing refineries five years to stop using it entirely.
Removes the EPA Administrator's waiver authority for this prohibition, so no refinery could get an exemption from the ban.
Sets a $37,500 civil penalty for each violation, giving the ban teeth.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 40 refineries that use hydrofluoric acid would pay the cost of converting to a safer alkylation method. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through gasoline prices, though the bill's findings say the alternative technology is commercially proven and already used at a majority of U.S. refineries.

drawbacks.text: Existing refineries would have only five years to convert, and the switch to a different alkylation process is a major capital project; some conversion cost could reach consumers at the pump.
The bill sets the violation penalty at $37,500 per violation, a level critics could argue is small relative to refinery revenues and the scale of the required investment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades real conversion costs at about 40 refineries against the risk of a catastrophic chemical release that the findings say could kill or permanently injure thousands within 25 miles. Because the safer alternative is already used at most U.S. refineries, the main honest objection is the five-year timeline and cost, not feasibility.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the same day, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Maxine Waters introduced the bill on February 4, 2026, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it in the record.

The bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to bar hydrofluoric acid at new refineries immediately and at existing refineries five years after enactment, with a $37,500 per-violation civil penalty and no waiver possible.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has moved the bill; the status quo holds, meaning refineries keep using hydrofluoric acid and the 14 million people nearby keep the risk the bill describes. The refining industry is better off as long as the bill goes nowhere, since it avoids conversion costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Refineries using hydrofluoric acid, for now

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban hydrofluoric acid use at petroleum refineries.

for.name: Reps. Ted Lieu, Nanette Barragán, Robert Garcia, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill its seven-cosponsor base.

against.name: Rep. Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Petroleum refining industry
against.role: Operators of refineries that use hydrofluoric acid alkylation
against.what_they_did: Has a direct financial stake in avoiding a mandated five-year conversion to a more expensive alkylation process; no formal opposition appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee has taken no action.

industries.note: About 40 refineries would be forced to retire HF alkylation and invest in a safer alternative within five years, facing $37,500 penalties per violation if they don't. Their interest in keeping the cheaper process runs directly against the safety of the 14 million people living in the blast-and-vapor zone around their plants.

industries.industry: Sulfuric acid and alternative alkylation technology providers
industries.note: Refineries converting to commercially proven alternatives would need equipment, acid supply, and services, creating a market that grows only if communities get the safety protection the bill promises.

analysis.trajectory: This bill has the profile of most private members' bills: one-party sponsorship, a single committee referral, and no movement. Unless the Energy and Commerce Committee schedules a hearing or markup before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, it will die without a vote, as earlier versions of similar refinery-safety proposals have.
